530.source: Module 1.1 Foundations of Health Data Literacy
530.text: This module introduces the foundations of health data literacy: what health data is, the forms it takes, and its main sources. By the end of this module, you will be able to: define data literacy and core concepts related to health data. distinguish between the main types of health data. identify typical internal and external data sources used for key public health questions. You are not expected to become a data scientist, but you do need enough data literacy to use numbers responsibly in your daily work! Because of that, this module aims to build your confidence in working with data: recognising what you are looking at, knowing which questions to ask, and seeing how different data sources fit together in a health information system. Foundations of Data Literacy. Data literacy is the ability to read, understand, work with, and communicate data. But it is not limited to statistics or programming.

531.source: Module 1.1 Foundations of Health Data Literacy
531.text: Data literacy is the ability to read, understand, work with, and communicate data. But it is not limited to statistics or programming. At its core, data literacy means being able to: recognise what a dataset or indicator is showing. interpret basic tables, charts, and dashboards. ask questions about how data was produced and how reliable it is. explain key findings to others in plain language. For public health professionals, this might involve some of the following examples: Select each flash card to learn more. Scientific Manuscript. understanding a coverage report for a vaccination campaign. Policy Brief (Decision-Makers). reviewing a line list from an outbreak investigation. Public-Facing Documents (Media & Community). interpreting a dashboard that summarises routine health facility data. Data Literacy for Public Health Decision-Making. Every important public health decision is based at least in part on data - for example, deciding where to deploy outreach teams, which districts to prioritise for surveillance, or whether an outbreak is under control.

540.source: Module 1.1 Foundations of Health Data Literacy
540.text: A dataset is a collection of records, a variable is one type of information in it, and an indicator is a calculated summary measure. A dataset is one row, a variable is one spreadsheet, and an indicator is one patient. A dataset and an indicator are the same, but a variable is different. Which of the following is a step in the health data lifecycle? Hiring staff for the health ministry. Data collection using registers or electronic forms. Approving international travel for supervisors. Writing national health legislation. Data Types and Sources in Health. Now that you know the basics, let's look at how health data is organized and where it comes from, so you can better judge what a given dataset can and cannot tell you. Let's get into it! Types of Health Data by Structure. Health data can be organised in different ways. Its structure affects how easily it can be stored, linked, and analysed.

541.source: Module 1.1 Foundations of Health Data Literacy
541.text: Health data can be organised in different ways. Its structure affects how easily it can be stored, linked, and analysed. Here we consider three main types by structure. Select the tabs to learn more about each structure. Structured data is organised into a clear format, usually rows and columns with predefined variables. It is the easiest to analyse with standard tools. Examples in public health include: monthly facility reports entered into an HMIS - a Health Management Information System (for example, number of outpatient visits, deliveries, or vaccinations). a line list of suspected outbreak cases, with variables such as name, age, sex, address, date of onset, and laboratory result. laboratory test registers with fixed fields for patient ID, sample type, test requested, result, and date. Because structured data follows an agreed format, it is easier to check for completeness and consistency, aggregate across facilities or districts, and use for routine monitoring.

547.source: Module 1.1 Foundations of Health Data Literacy
547.text: These data are particularly valuable for estimating coverage, equity, and health outcomes at national or subnational level. They are usually of high methodological quality but are collected less frequently than routine data. Understanding where these different data originate is essential for judging how well they represent the situation you care about. You can differentiate between internal data generated within your organization and external data generated from other sources like National censures, WHO, UNICEF, etc. Let's have a look at their key differences. Select the tabs about the key differences. Internal data sources are generated within your own organisation or health system. Common internal sources include: facility registers and electronic records. routine HMIS reports from public sector facilities. programme monitoring data for specific interventions (for example, HIV, TB, malaria, immunisation). Internal data are often more detailed and more frequently updated. However, they may have gaps (such as missing reports from remote facilities) and quality issues that need active management.

550.source: Module 1.1 Foundations of Health Data Literacy
550.text: Internal sources are always higher quality than external sources. Internal sources are generated within your organisation; external sources are produced by others such as national statistics offices or international agencies. Internal sources are always clinical; external sources are always survey-based. Internal sources use paper; external sources use electronic systems. In practice, public health decisions often draw on a mix of internal and external data. For instance, a programme manager might use routine HMIS reports to see recent trends in service use, and a national survey to understand how coverage varies by wealth, geography, or gender. Recognising the strengths and limitations of each source helps you decide how much weight to give each one and where additional information is needed. You've now explored the foundations of health data literacy - what health data are, how they are structured and where they come from, and why this matters for decision-making. Let's briefly summarise the main points!

555.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
555.text: Data Governance in Public Health. Data governance refers to the organised system that guides how health data is handled from the moment it is collected to the moment it is archived. It defines who is responsible for data, who is allowed to access it, and what standards must be followed to protect it. Note / Key Message Icon. In public health, a data governance framework is essential because data often contains sensitive personal information and is shared across many programmes, institutions, and partners. Governance helps ensure that data is used ethically and legally, while creating the conditions for high-quality analysis and effective collaboration. Let's look at the core principles that lie at the heart of Data Governance. Core Principles of Data Governance. Although institutions vary, most governance frameworks rest on five core principles that shape how health data is managed. Explore the graphic to see what each principle means in practice.

556.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
556.text: Although institutions vary, most governance frameworks rest on five core principles that shape how health data is managed. Explore the graphic to see what each principle means in practice. Select the numbered items in the image to learn more. Data stewardship and ownership. Every dataset needs a clear "home" and someone who is accountable for its accuracy and maintenance. When ownership is unclear, errors accumulate and no one feels responsible for correcting them. Controlled access and responsible sharing. Not everyone needs to see or modify every dataset. Role-based access helps limit unnecessary exposure to sensitive information, while formal data-sharing agreements define how organisations exchange data safely and transparently. Privacy, confidentiality, and security. Governance also prioritises privacy, confidentiality, and security, especially when dealing with identifiable patient information. Strong security safeguards, such as encrypted storage or secure logins, protect individuals and uphold national regulations. Good governance ensures that data is collected and used in ways that respect legal requirements, institutional protocols, and community expectations.

560.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
560.text: Who has access, and why? Which risks feel most relevant where you work - unclear responsibilities, missing documentation, or perhaps too many people able to access sensitive data? Try to identify one or two simple actions that could strengthen governance in your setting. Even small improvements-such as clarifying who approves data corrections or ensuring regular backups-can make a meaningful difference. Data Quality and Quality Assurance. When we say that data are "good enough" for decision-making, we are talking about data quality. Data quality is the degree to which a dataset can be trusted to reflect reality and support sound conclusions. Poor-quality data may be misleading, incomplete, or out of date, and can easily drive weak or even harmful public health decisions. Key Data Quality Dimensions. To judge whether data are truly reliable, public health teams rely on a small set of essential data quality dimensions. Select the numbered items to learn more about essential data quality dimensions.

561.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
561.text: To judge whether data are truly reliable, public health teams rely on a small set of essential data quality dimensions. Select the numbered items to learn more about essential data quality dimensions. Accuracy is about how close recorded values are to the truth. Completeness looks at whether all expected records and key variables are present. Timeliness reflects how current the data are and whether they arrive in time to guide action. Consistency asks whether numbers agree across time, facilities, or systems. Validity checks that values follow agreed formats and codes, such as valid age ranges or standard diagnosis categories. Together, these dimensions give a simple checklist for judging whether data are ready to be used. Data Quality Assurance Processes. Data quality does not improve by itself; it improves because specific steps are built into daily work. The following example illustrates a typical 4-step quality assurance process for public healt data: Select the arrow symbols to swith between steps.

562.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
562.text: Data quality does not improve by itself; it improves because specific steps are built into daily work. The following example illustrates a typical 4-step quality assurance process for public healt data: Select the arrow symbols to swith between steps. Quality assurance starts with basic validation at the point of data entry-for example, forms or electronic systems that do not allow impossible dates or missing mandatory fields. After submission, supervisors or information officers review reports, compare them with previous periods, and follow up on unusual values or missing submissions. At intervals, teams may verify figures against source documents, such as clinic registers, and correct errors where needed. Feedback to facilities closes the loop: it explains what went wrong and helps prevent the same problems in future. Some programmes also organise more formal data quality audits, where selected indicators are systematically checked across several sites to identify common weaknesses. Even without advanced software, simple checks can reveal many issues.

563.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
563.text: Some programmes also organise more formal data quality audits, where selected indicators are systematically checked across several sites to identify common weaknesses. Even without advanced software, simple checks can reveal many issues. The following suggestions can help you identify the most common issues: Select the images to flip them around for more information, then select the arrows to move between the common issues. Looking for values outside expected ranges, such as negative ages or more deliveries than total admissions, can quickly flag obvious errors. Counting how many facilities reported, or how many records are missing key fields, highlights problems with completeness. Examining whether totals match the sum of their components, and whether indicators follow a plausible trend over time, helps detect inconsistencies. When routine data differ sharply from survey results or other external sources, this does not automatically mean one source is wrong, but it is a strong signal that further investigation is needed.

566.source: Module 1.2 Data Governance and Quality Assurance
566.text: Imagine you are working in the district health office of Kifaru District. Your team is reviewing data from the routine immunisation programme for children under one year of age. Four health centres report monthly on the number of children who received all recommended vaccines. For this exercise, you are given a small extract from the district's dataset covering three recent months. This is what you find: Looking at the extract, Health Centre A reports 145 fully immunised children in a month where the target population is 120. Which data quality concern does this raise first? The value may be higher than the true number of eligible children. For Health Centre C, there is no report for Month 2, and the Month 3 report was submitted 25 days after the due date. Which statement best describes the quality issues? The data are accurate but not valid. The data are complete but not timely.

577.source: Module 2.1 Data Wrangling and Reproducible Workflows
577.text: Introduction to data wrangling. Data wrangling is the process of transforming raw, messy data into an analysis-ready dataset. It includes all the practical work that sits between receiving a file and being able to use it to answer a question. In public health, this might involve preparing routine facility reports from different districts, harmonising outbreak line lists compiled by separate teams, or combining electronic health records with laboratory results. Raw inputs often contain gaps, inconsistencies, and confusing formats. If we analyse them as they are, we risk drawing the wrong conclusions. Data wrangling helps to make the dataset consistent, complete enough for the task at hand, and reliable for decisions that affect programmes and populations. Core Steps in Data Wrangling. You have already seen in Module 1 that health datasets often reflect real-world pressures: busy clinics, manual data entry, weak connectivity, and changing tools. The resulting issues with the data collected are systematically addressed by the five core steps of data wrangling: Select the arrows below to switch between steps.

578.source: Module 2.1 Data Wrangling and Reproducible Workflows
578.text: You have already seen in Module 1 that health datasets often reflect real-world pressures: busy clinics, manual data entry, weak connectivity, and changing tools. The resulting issues with the data collected are systematically addressed by the five core steps of data wrangling: Select the arrows below to switch between steps. First, you get to know the dataset. You identify its sources, scan the variables, and form a picture of how the data are organised. At this stage you might already notice missing months, unusual values, or unexpected column types, but you're not fixing everything right away. Next, you impose structure. This may involve standardising column names, ensuring that dates and numbers are stored in appropriate formats, and reshaping the data so that each row represents a meaningful unit, such as a patient, an event, or a facility-month. Clear structure makes later work safer and more efficient. You then move into cleaning.

587.source: Module 2.1 Data Wrangling and Reproducible Workflows
587.text: By contrast, reproducible workflows have the following advantages. They: make methods transparent,. automate repetitive tasks,. reduce the risk of accidental changes, and. allow teams to respond quickly when new data arrive. Ensuring that results can be verified, trusted and shared easily and quickly. Core principles of reproducible data work. Reproducible workflows do not require advanced technology. They are based on a few simple habits: Click on the image below to flip it over for more information, then click on the arrow to select the next part. Every step in the process should be written down. This allows others to understand how and why the analysis was performed in a particular way. Repeated tasks should be automated through scripts instead of manual copying and pasting. This reduces errors and makes it easier to consistently apply the same rules over time. Separation of raw and processed data. Always keep original datasets intact and unchanged.

599.source: Module 2.2 Exploratory Data Analysis and Implementation Python
599.text: M2.2 Exploratory Data Analysis and Implementation Python. In this module, you will learn how to use exploratory data analysis (EDA) to understand what your cleaned public health data show and to guide further analysis. You will also see how simple Python scripts can carry out basic data wrangling, EDA, and create summary statistics such as 2×2 tables. To get started, click on the "Start" button at the top of the page or on the first chapter below. Now that you've learned how to turn raw health data into a clean, well-documented dataset using reproducible workflows, you are ready for the next step - shifting your attention from repairing the data to exploring and describing them to understand what is really in your cleaned dataset. This is where exploratory data analysis (EDA) comes into play. We will then also have a brief look at how the same logic you applied manually in tools like Excel can be expressed in simple Python code snippets.

600.text: This is where exploratory data analysis (EDA) comes into play. We will then also have a brief look at how the same logic you applied manually in tools like Excel can be expressed in simple Python code snippets. By the end of this module, you will be able to: explain what exploratory data analysis (EDA) is and why it is important in public health. describe how to explore single variables and simple relationships between variables using basic summaries and tables. explain how EDA can reveal remaining data quality issues and guide further analysis. describe, in simple terms, how Python scripts can be used to carry out basic data wrangling, EDA, and produce summary statistics such as 2×2 tables. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). Once data have been cleaned and organised, the next step is to understand what story they tell. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) can help with that. What is EDA and why is it essential?

611.source: Module 2.2 Exploratory Data Analysis and Implementation Python
611.text: A small 2×2 version of this table is very common in public health when comparing, for example, exposed vs not exposed and diseased vs not diseased. These basic comparisons do not prove cause and effect, but they quickly highlight which groups stand out and where you may need to look more closely - both for public health interpretation and for remaining data quality issues. Now let's recap the most important information from this section together. Select the right answer to each question below. What is the main purpose of exploratory data analysis (EDA) in this module? To collect new health data from facilities. To repair raw data and correct obvious errors. To explore and describe a cleaned dataset using simple summaries, tables, and visuals. To build complex statistical models. Which of the following best describes the difference between data wrangling and EDA? Data wrangling is done in Excel, EDA only in Python.

612.source: Module 2.2 Exploratory Data Analysis and Implementation Python
612.text: Which of the following best describes the difference between data wrangling and EDA? Data wrangling is done in Excel, EDA only in Python. Data wrangling repairs and organises the data; EDA interprets the cleaned data and checks what it shows. Data wrangling looks at relationships between variables; EDA looks only at single variables. Data wrangling is optional, EDA is not. Why might you create a two-way table (for example, age group by high blood pressure yes/no)? To remove all missing values from the dataset. To compare how an outcome is distributed across groups and quickly see which groups stand out. To convert categorical variables into numbers. To check whether the file was imported correctly. You have now seen how EDA helps you make sense of a cleaned dataset by using simple summaries, tables, and comparisons between groups. In the next step, we will look at how the same logic can be written into short Python scripts, so that data wrangling and EDA can be carried out automatically and reproducibly.

In the code above: df['high_bp'] creates a new column that is True if systolic blood pressure is 140 or higher, and False otherwise. pd.crosstab counts how many patients fall into each combination of high_bp (yes/no) and data_source (app/EHR), giving you a 2×2 table similar to what we built manually in Excel. You've now seen how EDA helps you make sense of a cleaned dataset and how simple Python scripts can automate key steps in data wrangling and analysis. Let's quickly recap the key takeaways! EDA starts after data wrangling and helps you understand what your cleaned dataset actually shows. Looking at one variable at a time (min, max, median, mean, distribution) helps you see what is typical, rare, or suspicious. Simple comparisons between variables (for example, age group by high blood pressure) show how outcomes differ between groups. Python scripts can repeat the same cleaning and EDA steps automatically, producing summaries and 2×2 tables in a reproducible way. Now that you've learned how to explore cleaned datasets with EDA and understood how simple Python scripts can support reproducible analysis, you're ready to focus on how to present these insights visually and see how they support real-world public health decision-making.

622.text: M3.1 Foundations of Data Visualisation. In this module, you will learn how to match different types of public health data to charts and maps. You will also see how core visualisations can reveal trends, differences, distributions, relationships and geographic patterns to support better decisions. To get started, click on the "Start" button at the top of the page or on the first chapter below. Now that you've learned how to clean, organise and explore data, you are ready to focus on how to show your findings clearly and convincingly. In this module, you will see how different types of visualisations match different kinds of public health questions. The goal is to give you enough conceptual understanding so that, in practice, you can choose appropriate visuals and interpret them confidently, even if someone else builds the dashboard or writes the code behind it. By the end of this module, you will be able to: explain why data visualisation is important for public health decisions. distinguish between different data types. describe which types of visualisation are appropriate for different data types and public health questions. interpret key messages from these visualisations.

623.text: The goal is to give you enough conceptual understanding so that, in practice, you can choose appropriate visuals and interpret them confidently, even if someone else builds the dashboard or writes the code behind it. By the end of this module, you will be able to: explain why data visualisation is important for public health decisions. distinguish between different data types. describe which types of visualisation are appropriate for different data types and public health questions. interpret key messages from these visualisations. Visualisation and Data Types in Public Health. Public health work generates large volumes of information: case counts, admissions, vaccination coverage, stock levels, survey responses and more. Reading these values only as tables is slow and makes important patterns easy to miss. Visualisation turns numbers into a picture the brain can process quickly. A chart or map summarises many data points in one view, so you can immediately see whether something is going up or down, which groups differ most, or whether anything looks unusual.

627.text: Discrete data are counts, such as number of malaria cases, births or outpatient visits. Continuous data can take any value in a range, such as haemoglobin level, blood pressure, age or incidence rate. Temporal (time-based) data describe how something changes over time (daily case counts, weekly admissions, monthly coverage, annual mortality). The order of observations matters. Spatial (geographic) data link information to a place (district-level HIV prevalence, facility coordinates, province-level immunisation coverage). It is important to understand these basics before we move on. Let's review the most important questions. Select the right answer to each question below. Why are visualisations especially important for public health staff? They replace the need for any further analysis. They make reports look more professional for external donors. They summarise complex data so busy staff can quickly see patterns and key messages. They allow staff to hide data quality problems from decision-makers. Which of the following is a good example of how visualisation supports public health decision-making?

629.text: It allows you to ignore categorical data and focus only on numerical data. It means you never need to think about the audience for the visualisation. In this section, you will see which chart types work best for different questions and data types. As you read, note what kind of data sits on each axis (or is encoded by colour or area): categorical, numerical, temporal or spatial. This will help you choose visuals for your own work. Let's get into it. Comparison charts answer questions such as "Which group has higher or lower values?" or "How do categories differ?". They typically combine categorical data (the groups) with numerical data (the values). There are 2 main charts used for this purpose. Select the chart headings below reveal more about each. Bar charts are one of the most useful tools in public health. They work best when you have categorical data on one axis (for example region, age group, sex) and numerical data on the other (for example number of cases, percentage coverage).

631.text: Bar charts are most effective when the number of categories is moderate and labels are clear. If your main interest is change over time, a line chart using temporal data is usually better. When you need to compare many regions, time periods or indicators, bar charts quickly become crowded. Heat maps provide a more compact overview. A heat map displays data as a grid of coloured cells. The rows and columns typically represent categorical and/or temporal data (for example districts by month), and the colour of each cell encodes a numerical value (such as case counts or coverage). By scanning the colours, you can spot hotspots and patterns across many groups and time periods at once, even though exact values are less visible. Heat maps are therefore better for recognising patterns across large tables of categorical and temporal data, while bar charts remain preferable for simple, precise comparisons between a few categories.

633.text: Distribution of Disease Type in Outpatient Visits. In public health, pie charts might also show, for example, how a programme budget is distributed across cost categories, or the proportion of outpatient visits due to different disease groups. However, as the number of categories increases, or when precise comparisons are needed, simple or stacked bar charts are usually more effective for showing proportions. Trend and Progression Charts. Trend charts answer questions such as "How does this indicator change over time?". They rely on temporal data on the horizontal axis and numerical data on the vertical axis. Line charts are the main tool for this. Values at regular time points (days, weeks, months) are plotted and then connected by a line. This makes it easy to see overall direction and timing of changes. The line chart of monthly COVID-19 cases below shows how infections rise to a peak and then fall again as control measures take effect.

634.text: This makes it easy to see overall direction and timing of changes. The line chart of monthly COVID-19 cases below shows how infections rise to a peak and then fall again as control measures take effect. In public health, such line charts are widely used for weekly case counts, monthly service use, or annual mortality rates. Several lines on the same chart may even allow comparisons between categorical groups (for example regions or age groups) across time, as long as the lines remain clearly distinguishable. Line charts work best when time intervals are regular and data are not too sparse. The previous charts show only one summary value for each category or time point. They answer questions like "Which region has more cases?" or "How has coverage changed over time?". However, to understand how values are spread within a category, we need distribution charts. They focus on the distribution of numerical data - for example age, blood pressure, length of stay or daily visits - often grouped by a categorical variable such as facility or disease type.

638.text: The coloured "boxes" cover the middle 50% of the range. As you can see, Malaria has the highest and most variable (spread out) number of visits, whereas diarrhoea and "other" conditions generally have fewer and more stable daily visits. Sometimes we want to know whether two numerical variables are related - for example, whether age is associated with blood pressure, or whether BMI is linked to physical activity. There are 2 main tools that are used for this purpose. Select the tabs below to reveal the information. A scatter plot is the basic tool. Each point represents one observation (for example a person), positioned according to its value on the x-axis and y-axis (both numerical). For example, age on the x-axis and blood pressure on the y-axis. Looking at all points together, you can see whether: higher values of one variable tend to go with higher or lower values of the other (positive/negative correlation). there are groups of similar points (clusters). • any points lie far away from the rest (outliers).

639.text: For example, age on the x-axis and blood pressure on the y-axis. Looking at all points together, you can see whether: higher values of one variable tend to go with higher or lower values of the other (positive/negative correlation). there are groups of similar points (clusters). • any points lie far away from the rest (outliers). In the plot below, each red dot is one person. The blue line is a trend line summarising the overall pattern. The dots are widely scattered and the line slopes only slightly downwards, so there is no strong relationship between age and blood pressure. At most, blood pressure decreases very slightly with age, with a lot of variation between individuals. When there are many numerical variables to compare, one scatter plot is not enough. Instead, a correlation heatmap would be the appropriate tool. It shows the strength of the relationship between each pair of numerical variables in a grid.

641.text: The dark red diagonal of 1s is each variable compared with itself and can be ignored. In the example below, most values, such as the slight negative correlation between age and systolic BP (-0.13), are close to zero, so the relationships in this dataset are generally weak. Both scatter plots and correlation heatmaps are exploratory tools. Visible patterns suggest possible associations, highlighting areas of interest. But, on their own, they do not prove causation. So far, regions have appeared only as labels on axes or rows. In practice, the geography itself matters as well: which districts border each other, which areas are remote, and where clusters of high risk occur. Geospatial visualisations link spatial data to numerical indicators and there are generally 2 main types to know of: Choropleth Map. The most common type is the choropleth map, where each administrative unit - such as a district or province - is shaded according to the value of an indicator, for example immunisation coverage or incidence of a disease.

649.text: In this module, we will focus on time-series analysis - one of the most important ways of tracking how indicators change over time - and on dashboards, which bring key indicators, charts and maps together in a single view. By the end of this module, you will be able to: explain the importance of time-series analysis in tracking public health trends and interventions. identify key features of time-series data. describe how dashboards combine multiple visualisations to support public health decision-making. apply best practices in dashboard design to ensure clarity, usability, and ethical data representation. Basics of Time-Series Data. In public health, one of the most important questions is not "How many cases do we have now?", but "How is this changing over time?". Time-series data answer this question by tracking the same indicator at regular time intervals. Because most routine surveillance and service data are time series, they sit at the heart of public health monitoring, outbreak detection and planning - and they dominate the charts you see on most dashboards.

651.text: Does a sudden change suggest an outbreak, a data problem or the effect of an intervention? For public health staff, this makes time series one of the most practical ways to decide whether the situation is getting better, worse or unexpectedly different from usual. Time Series in Practice. If you paid attention in the previous module, you will appreciate that the main visual tool for time series has to be the line chart. Time goes on the horizontal axis, the indicator on the vertical axis, and a line connects the values. This simple chart already shows level, trend, and often seasonality at a glance. However, there are 3 common enhancements to build on this. Select the enhancements below to learn more. Adding a moving average means, instead of only plotting each weekly value, you also plot an average of the last few weeks. This smoothed line reduces the effect of random ups and downs and makes the underlying trend easier to see.

653.text: When interpreting the data at hand, most public health time series will focus on a few basic features. Select the image to flip it for more information, then use the arrows to move between the features. Level - the overall height of the series. Does the indicator usually sit at a low, moderate or high level (for example, five cases per week versus 500)? Trend - the long-term direction. Is there a gradual increase, decrease or stable pattern over months or years (for example, declining maternal mortality, rising chronic disease admissions)? Seasonality - repeating patterns. Do values rise and fall in a regular cycle, such as diarrhoeal disease peaks every rainy season or influenza peaks each cold season? Unusual peaks or drops - deviations from the usual pattern. Do we see sudden spikes that may signal an outbreak, or sharp drops that might indicate stock-outs, strikes or access problems? Recognising these features helps you avoid overreacting to normal seasonal peaks, and instead focus on real changes that need investigation or action.

654.text: Do we see sudden spikes that may signal an outbreak, or sharp drops that might indicate stock-outs, strikes or access problems? Recognising these features helps you avoid overreacting to normal seasonal peaks, and instead focus on real changes that need investigation or action. Let's look at some real-world examples. Diseases like malaria or influenza often follow clear seasonal patterns, and time-series analysis can help us track their fluctuations over time. Select the arrows below to switch between examples. Monthly malaria case counts. Consider monthly malaria case counts for several years in the same district. A simple line chart may show regular peaks around the rainy season and lower values in dry months. Adding a moving average can highlight whether the overall level of cases is rising or falling across years, beyond the usual seasonal cycle. Weekly reports of measles or cholera. Similarly, weekly reports of measles or cholera cases can be plotted to monitor for sudden spikes.

659.text: At the centre are key performance indicators (KPIs). These are the small set of indicators that matter most for the dashboard's purpose, such as vaccination coverage, number of suspected outbreak alerts, stock-out rates or proportion of facilities reporting on time. To provide context, dashboards also include supplementary charts, tables and maps. Let's have a look at a fictional example dashboard! Select the numbered items in the image below to learn more. KPIs are often displayed as numbers, gauges or small summary charts so that users can immediately see whether performance is on, above or below target. Line charts show trends over time. Bar charts show comparisons between regions (or maybe facilities / districts, etc.) Geographic patterns. Maps show geographic patterns. Behind the scenes, dashboards are connected to data sources, such as routine health information systems, laboratory systems or survey databases. Good dashboards clearly indicate how up to date the data are and how often they are refreshed.

664.text: Be transparent. about uncertainty or data gaps - highlight data confidence and gaps in the visual or caption. Ensure visuals represent data honestly. e.g. avoid distorted axes - starting a bar chart's vertical axis at a value much higher than zero can exaggerate small differences, while compressing the axis can hide meaningful change. Respect sensitive topics: e.g. for mortality, HIV, status, etc. - avoid stigmatising language and don't expose individuals or small groups. Now let's reflect on the dashboard topic for a brief moment. Select the right answer to each question below. Which type of dashboard is best suited for tracking day-to-day performance and monitoring progress towards targets? None of the above. (Operational dashboards support day-to-day monitoring, such as tracking case notifications or vaccine stocks.) Dashboard Interactivity. What feature in a dashboard allows users to switch between different data indicators without leaving the dashboard? Hover-over tooltips. (View switching allows users to change the indicator displayed in a chart or map, without leaving the dashboard.) Best Practice for Dashboard Design.

668.text: In this module, we'll introduce you to Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) with the goal of giving you its conceptual understanding to recognise when and why to use this method. By the end of this module, you will be able to: define Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) and their role in public health. distinguish between logistic regression and Poisson regression based on the types of outcomes they model. prepare abstracts, posters, or slides that effectively communicate study findings. adapt scientific content into plain language for non-technical audiences. Through time-series analysis, you have learned how to identify basic patterns and trends in public health data over time and across places. Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) are the logical next step to make this analysis more sophisticated. They are statistical models that quantify which factors drive these patterns, clarify the relationships between risk factors and outcomes, and estimate how strongly different characteristics are associated with key health events.

669.text: Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) are the logical next step to make this analysis more sophisticated. They are statistical models that quantify which factors drive these patterns, clarify the relationships between risk factors and outcomes, and estimate how strongly different characteristics are associated with key health events. In practice, GLMs help you identify who is most at risk and predict important outcomes in a transparent and interpretable way. In public health, GLMs can be used to predict things like: Whether a person will get sick (yes or no),. How many disease cases will happen in a specific area,. Or how long a patient might stay in the hospital. What makes GLMs so useful is their flexibility. As you can tell by the examples above, they can handle different types of data. Select the images below to view more information on these different types of data. Binary outcomes. (e.g., sick or healthy).

670.text: Select the images below to view more information on these different types of data. Binary outcomes. (e.g., sick or healthy). Count data. (e.g., the number of disease cases). Continuous data. (e.g., healthcare costs or time). Think of a GLM as a tool that looks at various factors (like age, location, or risk factors) and helps us understand how those factors influence health outcomes. It's a method to help us make more advanced and informed predictions based on data. There are 2 major GLMs that are important in the context of public health: Logistic Regression and. We'll uncover them in the course of this module! Logistic regression is a type of GLM used when the outcome we are trying to predict has only two possible values- like yes/no, true/false, or success/failure. For example, it could be predicting whether someone gets sick or not, based on certain factors like age, lifestyle, or vaccination status.

674.text: Step 1 - Collecting Data. First, we gather data on the things we want to count (e.g., disease cases, hospital visits) and also collect data on factors that might influence these counts (like age, vaccination status, or location). Step 2 - Looking for Patterns. Poisson regression looks at the relationship between the factors (like age or vaccination) and the count of events (like the number of disease cases). In contrast to logistical regression, it looks at frequencies instead of probabilities - trying to identify how changes in those factors might influence how often the event happens. Step 3 - Calculating the Rate. Poisson regression calculates a rate - the number of events happening over a specific time period or in a specific area. This is like asking, "How many times is this event likely to happen, given these factors?" Step 4 - Making Predictions. Based on the factors, Poisson regression predicts how many times the event will happen.

679.text: However, it is usually critical to understand who is most at risk of severe outcomes as early as possible so that clinical and community actions can be prioritised. Start by designing posters and radio messages without looking at the data. Communication materials are important, but in an emergency they should be guided by data. You risk missing the people and places most in need if you do not first analyse who is at highest risk. Focusing on the question: „who is most at risk of dying if they get cholera?", our field teams send daily line lists. For each patient, they record: age and sex. district. whether there is safe drinking water at home. time from first symptoms to arrival at a health facility. outcome: survived or died. We need a model that can use these risk factors to estimate the chance of death. Logistic regression on the patient-level line list.

683.text: Now that we started protecting the high-risk patients, I need to look at which districts is going to be in need of support the most. The surveillance team has compiled: weekly case counts by district. district population. access to safe water and sanitation. whether chlorination campaigns have started. recent rainfall. My new question is: in which districts are case numbers likely to grow next week if we do nothing more? Which analysis is most appropriate now? Poisson regression using weekly case counts by district and the listed risk factors. Poisson regression is a GLM designed for count data, such as the number of cases per district per week. It can estimate how factors like water access, rainfall, and chlorination campaigns are related to case rates and predict where counts are likely to rise. Logistic regression using only the patient-level outcome (survived or died). Logistic regression is best for binary outcomes at individual level.

686.text: Ignoring these factors weakens the response. Public health professionals like Dr Ama use logistic regression to guide decisions about high-risk patients, while Poisson regression guides decisions about high-risk places. Together, these GLMs help move from "we have data" to "we know what to do next" in a real public health emergency. You've now been introduced to Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) - what they are, the types of outcomes they can handle, and how logistic and Poisson regression help you estimate risks, counts, and rates in public health. Let's briefly summarise the key ideas before you move on to the next set of advanced analytics. Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) link risk factors to health outcomes to estimate risks, counts, and rates. Logistic regression is used for binary outcomes - predicting whether an event (e.g. getting sick) is likely to happen. Poisson regression is used for count outcomes - predicting how often events (e.g. disease cases) occur over time or across places.

687.text: Logistic regression is used for binary outcomes - predicting whether an event (e.g. getting sick) is likely to happen. Poisson regression is used for count outcomes - predicting how often events (e.g. disease cases) occur over time or across places. You have reached the end of Module 4. You are now equipped with the essential skills to transform complex data into clear, concise, and highly persuasive documents, ensuring your research achieves maximum real-world impact. You can now write for scientists, policy-makers, and the public. In Module 5 (our final module), we will discuss the Publication and Collaboration Lifecycle.

688.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
688.text: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health. In the previous module on Generalised Linear Models (GLMs), you focused on explaining relationships and estimating risks using interpretable statistical models. In this Machine Learning module, you shift towards algorithms that learn complex patterns from data to make predictions - helping you forecast outcomes, flag high-risk cases, and support decisions in situations where traditional models may struggle. To get started, click on the "Start" button at the top of the page or on the first chapter below. In this module, you will take the next step in advanced analytics by exploring Machine Learning. Building on your understanding of GLMs, you will gain a conceptual understanding of what Machine Learning is, how it differs from traditional statistical models, and when it can help you use public health data to anticipate outcomes and support timely decisions. By the end of this module, you will be able to: define Machine Learning and describe how it complements traditional statistical methods in public health. distinguish supervised learning problems as classification or regression tasks, based on the type of outcome. explain in simple terms how decision trees and random forests learn from past data to make predictions. describe why validation, bias checks, and interpretability are important when applying Machine Learning models in public health.

695.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
695.text: The tree ends in a prediction, such as "high risk" or "low risk". Such machine-learning-generated decision trees are useful because they are easy to explain - you can literally draw them as a simple flow chart, transparent, as you can see exactly why the model made a particular decision, and often very close to how clinicians and programme managers already reason about risk in their day-to-day work. Random forests - many trees, one stable decision. A random forest is simply a large group of decision trees (often hundreds) that work together to make a more reliable prediction. For this to work, it is important that the generated trees are not identical. For any given dataset, a random forest therefore ensures that each tree sees slightly different data. Expand the headings to learn data. Different rows (patients, districts, weeks). For each tree, the algorithm draws a new dataset by picking rows one by one at random from the original data, each time allowing the same row to be picked again.

697.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
697.text: This means that each tree learns a slightly different pattern. When the model is now used on new data, each tree gives its own prediction (for example, high vs low risk, or an expected case count). The random forest combines the outputs of all its trees: for categorical outcomes, it takes a majority vote across the trees, and for numerical outcomes, it calculates an average. By aggregating many different trees in this way, it cancels out individual quirks and produces a more stable, reliable prediction. You can think of it like asking many clinical teams, each of whom has seen a slightly different set of cases and tends to focus on slightly different risk factors. When they all vote together, you get a more balanced judgement. Let's revisit the most important concepts before diving into questions of limitations in the next chapter. A decision tree is best described as: A model that randomly assigns risk levels to patients.

700.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
700.text: Could it introduce or reinforce bias? First, a model can easily look "excellent" on the same data it was trained on, simply because it has memorised many details instead of identifying learning patterns. This phenomenon is called overfitting. To avoid it, analysts usually split the data into the following 2 sets: A training set - used to build the model,. A test set - kept aside and only used at the end. The model is trained on the first set and then checked on the second. This shows how well it is likely to perform on data it has never seen before - new patients, facilities, or districts. In more advanced setups, analysts may use cross-validation, where the data are split in several different ways and results are averaged. Models can also reflect and even amplify existing inequalities. If rural facilities, certain age groups, or women are under-represented in the training data, predictions for these groups may be less accurate or systematically biased.

701.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
701.text: Models can also reflect and even amplify existing inequalities. If rural facilities, certain age groups, or women are under-represented in the training data, predictions for these groups may be less accurate or systematically biased. This can worsen gaps in access or quality if left unchecked. But there are also two practical issues - even with high data quality and training. Expand the headings to learn more about these practical issues. Complex models can be hard to explain. If clinicians and managers do not understand why a model flags a patient or district as "high risk", they may not trust or appropriately use its output. Services, reporting practices, and disease patterns evolve. A model that worked well last year may perform poorly today if it is not regularly reviewed and updated. In short, validation, bias checks, clear communication, and regular review are essential parts of quality assurance for machine learning in public health.

702.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
702.text: A model that worked well last year may perform poorly today if it is not regularly reviewed and updated. In short, validation, bias checks, clear communication, and regular review are essential parts of quality assurance for machine learning in public health. You've now been introduced to Machine Learning - how it differs from and complements GLMs, how it can be used to turn past data into practical risk scores and forecasts. You've also seen why validation, bias checks, interpretability, and regular updating are essential to keep these models safe and reliable for public health use. Let's briefly summarise the key ideas of this module! Machine Learning learns patterns from data to make predictions, especially with large or complex public health datasets. Supervised learning uses inputs (features) and known outcomes (labels) to train models that predict results for new cases. Decision trees use simple if-then questions to classify risk in a way that is transparent and easy to explain.

703.source: Module 4.2: Machine Learning (ML) for Public Health
703.text: Supervised learning uses inputs (features) and known outcomes (labels) to train models that predict results for new cases. Decision trees use simple if-then questions to classify risk in a way that is transparent and easy to explain. Random forests combine many decision trees and aggregate their outputs to give more stable, reliable predictions. Machine Learning algorithms and their outputs should always be validated, checked for bias, and regularly reviewed over time. You have reached the end of this module. You've now seen how Machine Learning uses structured public health data to learn patterns and make predictions that support planning and decision-making. In the final modul of this course, you'll extend this toolkit to unstructured data - text. You'll explore how Natural Language Processing (NLP) applies machine learning to reports, news, and clinical notes, turning them into structured signals that complement and enrich the data you receive through routine information systems.

704.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
704.text: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health. In the previous module on Machine Learning, you focused on using structured data to learn patterns and make predictions for public health decisions. In this NLP module, you shift towards methods that help computers work with unstructured text - such as reports, news, and social media - turning it into numeric representations that models can analyse and turn into actionable insights for surveillance, planning, and risk communication. 10 - 15 minutes. To get started, click on the "Start" button at the top of the page or on the first chapter below. In this module, you will take the next step in advanced analytics by exploring Natural Language Processing (NLP). You will gain a conceptual understanding of how NLP helps computers work with unstructured text and turn it into usable information. You'll see how simple NLP pipelines and basic text representations can support outbreak detection, summarise large volumes of narrative reports, and provide insights into community perceptions for better public health decision-making.

705.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
705.text: You will gain a conceptual understanding of how NLP helps computers work with unstructured text and turn it into usable information. You'll see how simple NLP pipelines and basic text representations can support outbreak detection, summarise large volumes of narrative reports, and provide insights into community perceptions for better public health decision-making. By the end of this module, you will be able to: define Natural Language Processing (NLP) and describe its role in turning unstructured text into usable data for public health. describe a simple NLP pipeline that converts raw text into numerical representations for analysis. distinguish between Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF as basic methods for representing text as numbers. identify key public health applications of NLP, including event detection, topic clustering, and sentiment or perception monitoring. So far, we have mostly looked at numbers in tables - cases, ages, test results. But in public health, a lot of important information is written as text: doctors' notes, incident reports, call-centre logs, situation reports, news articles, and social media posts.

707.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
707.text: A panel with coloured clusters of small document icons: one cluster in blue, one in green, one in orange, etc. A small line chart with 2-3 coloured lines representing topics/signals. In public health practice, this can support outbreak detection by scanning news sites or online reports for early signs of unusual disease activity before formal notifications arrive. Furthermore, it can help monitoring health trends by analysing social media or other text sources to see how communities talk about symptoms, services, or interventions. How NLP Turns Text into Data. To make text useful for analysis, NLP follows a few simple steps. How NLP Turns Text into Data. Think of it as a small "factory line" that turns unstructured text into numbers a computer can work with. Select the arrows below to switch between steps. Step 1 - Start with raw text. We begin with real-world text: a doctor's note, a hotline log, a media report, or a batch of incident descriptions.

714.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
714.text: Tracking how often key outbreak-related terms appear over time. In practice, you usually start by counting how often each word appears (Bag-of-Words), and then use TF-IDF to give extra weight to the words that carry the most information. This creates simple, easy-to-interpret numeric "fingerprints" for each text that other models can then use to support public health surveillance and decision-making. Let's recap here before we navigate through a real-life example in the next chapter! What does the Bag-of-Words (BoW) approach do with a text? It analyses grammar and word order to understand full sentences. It translates the text into different languages. It ignores grammar and word order and simply counts how often each word appears. It removes all repeated words so that each word appears only once. How does TF-IDF change the way words are represented compared with simple counts? It gives higher weight to very common words that appear in many documents.

715.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
715.text: How does TF-IDF change the way words are represented compared with simple counts? It gives higher weight to very common words that appear in many documents. It gives higher weight to words that appear often in a specific document but less often across all documents. It assigns the same weight to every word, regardless of how often it appears. It removes all rare words from the dataset. Why are Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF useful in public health NLP applications? They allow models to store the original text without any processing. They automatically correct spelling mistakes in clinical notes. They turn each document into a numeric "fingerprint" that models can use for tasks like classification, clustering, and event detection. They replace the need for any numeric data from surveillance systems. Scenario: NLP Applications in Public Health. When a sudden cholera outbreak starts in a coastal African country, Dr Nala at Africa CDC is called to support the national response.

716.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
716.text: Scenario: NLP Applications in Public Health. When a sudden cholera outbreak starts in a coastal African country, Dr Nala at Africa CDC is called to support the national response. She sits in the emergency operations centre, looking at fast-changing numbers on the screen. Help her navigate through this difficult situation! Using NLP to Support an Outbreak Response and Vaccination Campaign. Nala, a surveillance officer at Africa CDC, in using text data to guide decisions before and during an outbreak. I am on duty in the Africa CDC situation room. Formal surveillance reports look normal, but several colleagues mention local news stories about "unexplained deaths" and "severe diarrhoea" in one Member State. We have an NLP system connected to online news sites and situation reports. What should I do first? Configure the NLP system to track words such as "cholera", "unexplained deaths", and "bloody diarrhoea", combine them with place names and dates, and review any unusual spikes it flags.

718.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
718.text: Ask one staff member to manually read as many news sites as possible each day and send me any worrying headlines by email. Manual scanning of many news sites is slow, tiring, and inconsistent. It is better to let NLP filter and flag potential events, so staff can focus on interpreting the most relevant items. After a few days, the NLP dashboard shows a sudden spike in news items mentioning "bloody diarrhoea" and a particular district name, far above the usual background level. Formal case reports from that district are still low. How should I respond? Treat this as an early signal, contact the Member State focal point, and request more information and verification from the district. NLP-based alerts from news and reports are early warning signals. They should trigger closer scrutiny and communication with national counterparts, not automatic public declarations. Announce a confirmed cholera outbreak at regional level based on the news spikes alone.

725.source: Module 4.3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Public Health
725.text: It is better to acknowledge them openly and provide clear, credible information. Public health professionals like Dr Nala use NLP to scan text for early event signals, summarise thousands of reports into key themes, and understand community perceptions around interventions. Together, these applications help turn unstructured words into timely, actionable insights that strengthen surveillance, response, and risk communication. You've now been introduced to Natural Language Processing (NLP) and how methods like Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF feed into practical applications. Let's briefly summarise the key ideas of this module! Natural Language Processing (NLP) helps computers turn unstructured text - such as notes, reports, news, and social media - into usable data for public health. NLP follows simple steps: start with raw text, break it into pieces, clean it, turn words into numbers, and then apply models. Bag-of-Words counts how often each word appears in a text, creating a basic numeric fingerprint for each document.
